---

## The question {#origins-1}

::: {.origin-block}
A common view in family policy: **inflation hits families with children harder.** They buy more groceries, child care, cars and school supplies, and those prices jumped after 2021.
:::

Headline CPI tracks the spending of urban consumers. So we built two baskets from surveyed expenditures: one for families with children, the other for single-person and other households, each priced with the same national CPI item indexes.

**Did the family basket get more expensive, faster?**

---

## Two forces pull in opposite directions {#origins-2}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Families spend a bigger share on:**

- Child care
- Groceries
- Cars and gas
- Education
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Single households spend a bigger share on:**

- Rent (12.7% of the budget, against 5.3% for families)
- Electricity
- Tobacco
:::

::::

::: {.callout-box}
We measure one mechanism: whether the *mix* of what a household buys gives it a different inflation rate. Everyone faces the same price for a given item here. BLS's experimental index for older Americans (CPI-E) works the same way.
:::

---

## The budgets {#cex-1}

The **Consumer Expenditure Survey** is BLS's survey of household spending. We use its published annual averages by household type, the same survey BLS uses to weight the CPI.

::: {.callout-box}
"Families with children" pools married couples with children of any age (30.3 million households in 2024) and single parents with a child under 18 (6.2 million), weighted by how many households are in each. The main comparison group is single-person and other households (64.4 million); we also check against all households and married couples without children.
:::

- 41 spending categories, every year from 1988 to 2024
- Each category checked against the survey's own published totals: 201 checks, no failures
- Standard errors from BLS's published tables, so every comparison carries a margin of error

---

## Where the budgets differ {#cex-2}

![](`r fig_slide("f01_budget_diff_slide.png")`){.r-stretch}

::: {.chart-note}
Family budget share minus single-household share, 2024. Rent is the largest difference by far.
:::

---

## Pricing the budgets {#crosswalk-1}

Each of 37 spending categories is matched to the official CPI series for it, 62 series in all. Categories like "vehicles" combine several (new, used, leased) the way BLS combines them.

::: {.callout-box}
**Owners' housing is priced the way CPI prices it.** CPI charges homeowners what their home would rent for. The survey asks every owner that question, and BLS uses the answer to weight the CPI. We use the same answer.
:::

Built this way, our all-household index differs from official CPI by 0.1 percentage point on average across 12-month rates. This checks the aggregate fit, but cannot test prices paid within each household type.

---

## The result {#result-main}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
![](`r fig_slide("cumulative_slide.png")`){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
| Dec 2019 to Jul 2026 | |
|---|---|
| Families with children | **+29.4%** |
| Single-person and other | **+30.1%** |
| **Gap** | **−0.7 pts** |

About 0.1 point a year, and in families' favor. The corrected 95% sampling margin is about ±0.4 to ±1.0 points, depending on how errors carry across survey years.
:::

::::

::: {.callout-box}
**No meaningful excess from the spending mix.** Across nine baskets the family-minus-single/other gap runs from −1.0 to +0.1 points. Other price inputs, family definitions and index formulas leave that conclusion intact. Prices paid within items are outside this index.
:::

---

## Compared with whom? {#comparators}

![](`r fig_slide("comparators_slide.png")`){.r-stretch}

::: {.chart-note}
The largest negative gap is against single-person and other households, whose basket has more housing. Against all households the gap is −0.2 points; against married couples without children, who spend more on slow-rising medical care, it is +0.2. Neither is outside the margin of error. **These group baskets have similar inflation.**
:::

---

## 2021-22: a blip, then a reversal {#two-waves}

![](`r fig_slide("gap12_slide.png")`){.r-stretch}

::: {.chart-note}
Twelve-month inflation, families minus single-person and other households, with an approximate 95% sampling interval. From April 2021 to August 2022 the family basket ran up to 0.6 points hotter, but over those two years the difference added up to +0.2 points, too small to separate from survey error. From late 2022 rent took over and the single/other basket ran clearly hotter, by 0.65 points over 2023-24. By July 2026 the gap was zero.
:::

---

## Normal times look the same, only more so {#result-normal}

![](`r fig_slide("blocks_slide.png")`){.r-stretch}

::: {.chart-note}
Contribution of each spending area to the gap. From 2014 to 2019, before COVID, families trailed singles by 1.05 points. Rent rose 20% while overall prices rose 9%, and singles spend more than twice the share on rent. Cars and clothes, which families buy more of, got cheaper.
:::

---

## Income sorts inflation; family type barely does {#result-income}

![](`r fig_slide("income_bars_slide.png")`){.r-stretch}

::: {.chart-note}
::: {.callout-box}
Same method, same years. The lowest-income tenth of households saw prices rise 2.1 points more than the top tenth. The family gap is a third that size and runs the other way. BLS's own research index by income finds a similar gap: +2.1 points for the bottom versus top fifth, Dec 2019 to Dec 2025, against our +1.8.
:::
:::

---

## Why (1): a rate averages shares, not dollars {#intuition-0}

Families spend $105,000 a year to single households' $57,000. That gives them a bigger dollar hit. It does not give them a faster rate. A household that buys twice as much of the same basket has the same inflation rate.

The rate depends on budget *shares*, and the shares are close:

::: {.callout-box}
73% of the family budget sits in categories where family and single shares differ by less than 1 percentage point. Only five categories differ by more: **rent, vehicle purchases, education, child care, groceries.**
:::

---

## Why (2): buying more only matters if the price outran average {#intuition-1}

![](`r fig_slide("scatter_slide.png")`){.r-stretch}

::: {.chart-note}
A category moves the gap when families buy more of it **and** its price rose faster than everything else. Rent, far to the left, pulled families down most. Education (tuition up 14% against 30% overall) pulled them down too, but that is mostly parents of college-age children. Gasoline pushed them up. Child care sits on the zero line.
:::

---

## Why (3): child care rises like any other service {#intuition-childcare}

![](`r fig_slide("childcare_services_slide.png")`){height=330}

::: {.chart-note}
:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
Since 2010 day care prices have risen at the same pace as services overall (in the 2000s they ran faster). Services are mostly labor, and labor costs climb faster than goods prices. In the 2010s day care beat overall inflation only because goods prices barely moved.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-box}
The problem is the size of the bill. Married couples whose oldest child is under 6 average **$5,586 a year** on child care, 6.4% of spending, and that average includes families who pay nothing.
:::
:::

::::
:::

---

## Why (4): housing has economies of scale {#intuition-housing}

![](`r fig_slide("size_slide.png")`){.r-stretch}

::: {.chart-note}
A family of four needs one kitchen and one roof. Housing takes 40% of a one-person household's spending and 31% of a four-person household's: about $19,900 per person against $7,800. Groceries and cars take the extra share. Since housing rose fastest, the household with the bigger housing share got the higher inflation rate.
:::

---

## Similar rates, very different bills {#burden}

| | Inflation, Dec 2019 to Jul 2026 | Extra cost per year for the 2019 non-housing basket | Share of spending on groceries, utilities and housing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Married couple with children | 29.3% | **$16,300** | 36.6% |
| Single-person and other | 30.1% | $8,100 | 43.3% |
| One parent, child under 18 | 30.2% | $9,500 | **43.0%** |
| *Lowest-income fifth (reference)* | 30.5% | $5,800 | 46.3% |

::: {.callout-box}
The extra cost of the fixed 2019 non-housing basket is twice as large for married families as for the single/other group, at a slightly lower rate. Single parents have a necessity share closer to the bottom income fifth than to married couples. The index alone cannot measure hardship.
:::

---

## What this does not cover {#limits}

- **Prices paid.** Everyone is charged the same price for the same item here. Scanner-data research finds households pay quite different prices within an item.
- **Cash versus CPI housing costs.** Owners are charged their home's rental value, as in CPI. An owner with a locked-in mortgage saw cash housing costs rise less than that; a recent buyer saw them rise more.
- **Age.** Families average 44 years old, single households 53. The published tables don't allow controlling for age, and the comparison with childless couples shows age matters through medical care.
- **Survey error.** Margins of error use BLS expenditure standard errors, with category errors treated as uncorrelated. Under the cross-year correlation bound, the headline gap is not distinguishable from zero.
- **Index formula.** The headline uses two-year-old spending weights, following CPI practice since 2023. An annual-share Törnqvist check, which approximates the chained CPI concept, gives a smaller gap: −0.5 rather than −0.7.

::: {.notes}
Revised 2026-09-23 after two methods reviews. The earlier version headlined 25.32% vs 25.26%. That basket priced health insurance premiums with a CPI index that fell 19% while CPI rose 30%, and left out owners' housing. Review 2 added comparison groups, family definitions, a superlative index and a BLS benchmark (docs/review_checks.md). Methods and decisions: docs/decisions_log.md D-27 to D-40.
:::
